evidence: Caes. BG 4.2.6: vīnum omnīnō ad sē importārī nōn patiuntur
Caes. BG 5.12.5: aere ūtuntur importātō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Also, figuratively, to bring on something unwelcome: calamitātem alicui importāre (Cic. Sest. 146, Lewis & Short). It never means “matter” or “be important”: that is rēfert or interest (see important).
To carry in by cart or ship. In the passive it is also to ride or sail in, and invehī in aliquem is to attack someone in words (Lewis & Short).
Cicero’s noun, beside exportātiō (see export). Later Latin also used it for an invective (Lewis & Short).
Coming from outside, foreign (Lewis & Short): imported goods are mercēs adventīciae. Its other common sense is “extraordinary, not regular” of income (pecūnia adventīcia, a windfall).

phrases.latin: Vīnum omnīnō ad sē importārī nōn patiuntur, quod eā rē ad labōrem ferendum remollēscere hominēs atque effēminārī arbitrantur.
phrases.english: They do not allow wine to be imported at all, because they think it makes men soft and unmanly in bearing hardship.

phrases.latin: inportantur nōn mercēs sōlum adventīciae sed etiam mōrēs
phrases.english: it is not only foreign goods that are imported, but foreign ways as well

sources: Lewis & Short: importo · Lewis & Short: inveho · Lewis & Short: invectio · Lewis & Short: adventicius
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. import (foreign goods).
Caesar and Cicero checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (11 November 2026); the quotation from the Republic keeps that edition’s spelling inportantur.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
